verses.verse:
तन्तु वाद्ये भवेत्कम्पः नेत्राभ्याम् स विलोक्यते।
वायु वाद्ये तु यः कम्पः सोऽनुमानेन बुध्यते।६३।
verses.text: In a tantu vādya (stringed instrument) there is kampa (vibration), and it is seen with the eyes; but the vibration in a vāyu vādya (wind instrument) is understood by inference.

commentary.text: That is, in instruments such as the vīṇā and the sitar the string is made to vibrate by the hand, so we can see that kampana (vibration) with our eyes. But the flute is a vāyu vādya (wind instrument): the air from the mouth sets up vibration in the air inside the flute, so we can establish that vibration only by reasoning (anumāna, inference). For it is a scientific truth that nāda (musical sound) cannot arise without vibration. Only a thing that has lacāva (elasticity) can vibrate. A string has elasticity, so it vibrates. Air too has elasticity, so it vibrates. But the vibration of a string differs from the vibration of air in direction. If the string's vibration is across its width, the air's vibration is along its length. The string's length is tied to the pegs and is tightened, but the air's width is bound and held tight by the bamboo. So if the bamboo cracks for some reason, the air is no longer held tight and no sound is produced. Like air, water too is elastic, so the jal taraṅg is a successful instrument. But water cannot vibrate without the support of air, and in the same way a string does not vibrate without the support of air. So for vibration the support of air has to be taken. In the flute, air is made to vibrate by air, in air. In stringed instruments, material is made to vibrate by material, in air. In instruments such as the shehnai, material is made to vibrate by air, in air. In covered instruments (such as the mṛdaṅga), skin is made to vibrate by the hands, in air. The saying (jātaḥ prāṇāgni saṃyogāt) [it is born from the union of breath and fire] is a scientific truth.
